idiom_name: std::variant canonical message with a std::visit normalizer
implementation_notes: The canonical message is modelled as a closed std::variant<CsvRecord, XmlRecord, KvRecord> and each per-format mapping as an overload-set visitor passed to std::visit, which replaces the Translator class hierarchy and its registry with one dispatch point the compiler checks for completeness; the parsers themselves stay hand-written because the standard library ships no serialization (nlohmann/json or Boost.JSON is the usual third-party choice when JSON is one of the formats). The classic virtual-MessageTranslator-plus-registry form remains right when translators are configured or registered at run time, when the format set must stay open across translation units or shared libraries, or when a C++03/ABI-stable interface is required. Prefer the variant form when the format set is closed and known at compile time, precisely because adding an alternative then makes every non-exhaustive visitor fail to compile.
pitfalls: A visitor without an overload for every alternative fails to compile - do not silence that with a catch-all [](const auto&) lambda, which reintroduces the missing-translation bug at run time.

std::variant construction prefers the first alternative that accepts the argument, so a parser helper returning something convertible (a const char* that decays to bool) can silently select the wrong alternative; give each parser its own return type.
Passing the variant through the normalizer by value deep-copies the canonical message; take it by const reference and move the result out.

variants.name: Abstract MessageTranslator hierarchy with a registry (classic OO)
variants.idiom_name: abstract MessageTranslator plus std::map registry of owning pointers
variants.implementation_notes: The pattern's classic realization: an abstract MessageTranslator with virtual CanonicalMessage translate(const RawMessage&) const, one derived class per source format, and a registry keyed by the detected tag that the router consults. Choose it when translators must be registered at run time (plugins, generated bindings), when the set of formats is open across translation units, or when an ABI-stable C++03 interface is required. It costs a virtual call plus a heap allocation per translation and loses the compiler's exhaustiveness check, so a missing registry entry becomes a runtime error path that must be handled explicitly.
pitfalls: Registry misses surface at run time, not at compile time - which is exactly the failure the variant form eliminates; if you keep the classic form, add a start-up test that asserts every known tag resolves.
The registry owns the translators by unique_ptr, so it must outlive the normalizer; a registry holding references to destroyed statics is a shutdown-order bug.
Replacing explicit detection with dynamic_cast or typeid tests introduces a second, implicit routing mechanism; keep the tag decision in one place.
